structure.title: Prologue and parodos · A conversation before daylight
structure.text: Two sisters must decide what to do about their brother's exposed body. Before Creon delivers his account of a city's needs, we have already heard the edict translated into a particular task somebody must perform or abandon.

structure.title: First episode – second stasimon · The decree finds its defendant
structure.text: A guard brings unwelcome news. When Antigone stands before Creon, the facts are easier to establish than the authority under which she acted. Ismene's attempt to share responsibility makes even solidarity a matter for dispute.

structure.title: Third and fourth episodes · Advice to a ruler
structure.text: A son and then a seer approach Creon with warnings. Their different ways of speaking expose the difficulty of advising a ruler who hears disagreement as a bid for mastery. Meanwhile his orders are being carried out.

people.name: Antigone and Ismene
people.text: They have lost the same brothers. Antigone knows what she owes the dead. Ismene counts the remaining lives that may be lost, including the sister she loves.

people.name: Creon
people.text: After civil war he wants the city to make an unmistakable distinction between its defender and its attacker. Their common sister presents him with a duty that survives his distinction.

context.title: What a handful of dust can do
context.text: Burial rites mark a duty to the dead. A small, repeatable act can therefore violate a public prohibition. The guard's difficulty in keeping a corpse uncovered helps turn a dispute about authority into a piece of stage action.

notice.text: Listen for the public opinion nobody hears publicly.
notice.why: Haemon offers his father an account of what citizens say out of earshot. The king's ability to silence dissent has made it harder for him to know what the city thinks.

notice.text: Watch the guard trying to get away alive.
notice.why: His halting, self-interested speech shows how an order sounds to the man charged with enforcing it. He has absolutely no wish to become the next great example of courage.

opening: Antigone's brother has been declared a traitor, and the new ruler forbids anyone to bury him. Leaving his body exposed will demonstrate that the city has a government again. Antigone intends to bury him anyway. Both understand the public meaning of what they are doing, and neither thinks the other has the right to decide. Sophocles brings political authority into collision with an obligation that cannot be voted away, while a ruler's need to appear firm steadily narrows his ability to hear advice.
